title: Drinking Wine Has Lower Death Risk than Beer, Spirits
paragraphs: Alcohol is linked with many health impacts, including heart disease, cancer and early death. According to the World Health Organization, there is no safe level of alcohol consumption.
However, a study in Nutrition Journal has found that beer, spirits and wine don't have the exact same health risks — with low to moderate wine consumption carrying a lower mortality risk.

The research included 340,000 participants from the UK Biobank health database. The researchers looked at alcohol consumption rates among the participants, as well as the number and causes of deaths among them over 13 years.

High consumption of any alcoholic drink was linked with higher death rates from all causes. The researchers defined high consumption as more than 40 grams of pure alcohol a day for men, and over 20 grams a day for women.
For reference, there are around 20 grams of pure alcohol in a 500 milliliter bottle of 5% beer.
Moderate alcohol consumption, meaning 20 to 40 grams a day for men and 10 to 20 grams for women, was also linked with higher death rates from cancer.
However, the type of alcohol people consumed seemed to matter when they were drinking less of it.
Beer and cider were linked with a higher risk of cancer death even at low-level consumption — up to 20 grams a day for men, and up to 10 grams a day for women.
Non-consumption was defined as having no more than 20 grams of alcohol a week.
At both low and moderate levels, drinking spirits was also linked with an increased risk of death by any cause.
However, low-level wine consumption was linked with a lower mortality risk from any cause, and red wine specifically was associated with a lower risk even at moderate levels.
The mortality risk increased for high wine consumption, though. The researchers also warn that this study is only observational, and doesn't prove that wine can protect health.
